| Dissent in part, joining Parts II, III-A, III-B and IV | Stevens | — | Would grant retrospective Ex Post Facto relief; otherwise joins the indicated process disposition | Punitive-operation objection; conditional process joins when civil notification remains available |
| Concurrence in part in the judgment and dissent in part | Scalia | Thomas in full; O'Connor and Kennedy on proof quantum only | Rejects punishment relief; would remove heightened proof while retaining State persuasion and advance review | Separate successive-criminal-prosecution ground and preponderance process ground; joins Parts II and IV |

#### Holdings

### I. The challenged notification is not punishment on this record

**Holding and operative rule:** For the class whose offenses preceded October 31, 1994 and who face Tier 2 or Tier 3 notification, New Jersey's civil public-protection purpose remains unrebutted by the clearest proof of punitive purpose or effect in the scheme's supported combined operation. The challenged notification therefore supplies no Ex Post Facto or Double Jeopardy ground for relief; the Court decides no same-offense question.

**Authority:** Part I of Souter's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer; six Justices directly adopt the common civil-classification ground. Scalia and Thomas support rejection on their separate grounds; Stevens dissents on Ex Post Facto punishment and does not reach independent Double Jeopardy identity.

**Controlling explanation:** Ursery supplies civil intent followed by demanding contrary proof, and Hendricks and Hudson require examination of actual combined operation. A civil label is insufficient. Here risk grading, individual exceptions and audience tailoring connect the warning to public protection. Tier 2 reaches qualifying schools, child-care facilities and organizations serving children or supporting women, subject to the state court's likely-encounter construction; Tier 3 reaches members of the public likely to encounter the registrant. The scheme directly imposes no residence, movement, employment or licensing prohibition.

The contrary shaming argument is substantial. Government actively distributes conviction and predicted-danger information, with potentially severe effects on housing, employment, relationships and safety. Those consequences cannot be dismissed categorically because some involve private acts. But the supported tailoring and causal record do not establish the clearest proof of punishment. The reported nineteen experiences, six state-compelled disclosures and separate 135-notification figure cannot be merged into one incidence calculation. Confidentiality instructions for Tier 2 and warnings against threats, vandalism and assault matter without guaranteeing perfect containment.

Hendricks found a different cumulative operation: prisonlike additional custody sustained on a future treatment structure. Its punitive result supplies no automatic classification of notification, just as its civil designation supplied no immunity there. Hudson and Kurth Ranch preserve meaningful aggregate examination; Halper's personal-monetary-penalty accounting is not a notification formula. The holding neither makes reputation irrelevant nor treats every public-safety measure as civil. Materially different punitive operation remains a different case. Registration alone, Tier 1, post-enactment offenses and every later registry are not decided.

### II. The State must justify both tier and notification plan before ordinary notification

**Holding and operative rule:** In the ordinary circumstances presented, Tier 2 or Tier 3 notification may not proceed without a meaningful advance opportunity to contest both the risk classification and the proposed notification plan, with the prosecutor bearing persuasion for each. The protected interest rests on New Jersey's substantive restriction requiring disclosure to serve a legitimate and substantial interest with minimized invasion, rather than on reputation alone or a promise of procedures.

**Authority:** Part II of Souter's opinion, joined by all seven other Associates; eight Justices directly adopt this protected-interest, hearing and State-persuasion ground. Stevens joins conditionally because civil notification remains available under the Court's judgment. Stone-Zsela supports the disposition on his stated procedural grounds without joining this distinct state-entitlement explanation.

**Controlling explanation:** Sandin directs attention to a real substantive constraint and meaningful deprivation; its prison setting supplies no universal noncustodial threshold. Paul v. Davis distinguishes reputation alone, which is not the sole interest here. The actual state disclosure restraint and irreversible distribution make erroneous classification or an excessive audience a protected deprivation.

Mathews requires consideration of the interest, error risk and practical burdens. The State selects the tier and audience and already assembles an initial case. Requiring the registrant ultimately to disprove that justification wrongly allocates the risk of an unsupported disclosure. A prosecutorial prima facie presentation does not replace the State's ultimate persuasion on both determinations. Public protection and prompt warning remain substantial interests, but do not justify making the affected person disprove the affirmative basis for disclosure.

Individual review must permit challenges to factual accuracy and calculation, atypical cases and excessive plans. A credible supported indication of likely reoffense requires high-risk treatment regardless of score; a physical condition minimizing risk, including advanced age or debilitating illness, requires low-risk treatment regardless of score. The Scale is not conclusive. This individual proceeding does not authorize a new facial attack on the Scale or its weights. No individual tier or plan is approved, and no general federal informational-privacy right is decided. The distinct proof-quantum question is addressed below.

### III. Risk classification requires clear and convincing proof; the plan injunction is retained on a narrower authority basis

**Holding and operative rule — risk classification:** Before the ordinary Tier 2 or Tier 3 notification presented here, the State must establish the factual basis and risk classification by clear and convincing evidence. Preponderance alone is constitutionally insufficient for that classification in this setting; proof beyond a reasonable doubt and certainty of future conduct are not required.

**Authority:** Part III-A of Souter's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer; five direct supporters. Stevens's join operates because the Court permits civil notification. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would hold State preponderance sufficient.

**Controlling explanation:** Mathews requires a practical comparison of error risks, not automatic transplantation of every civil burden. Addington and Santosky show that a civil label does not end the inquiry and that sufficiently serious erroneous deprivation can require greater assurance. The classification here combines disputed historical facts, unadjudicated circumstances and predictive judgments with disclosure that cannot effectively be recalled. Overclassification can alter housing, work, safety and status before an error is repaired.

Underclassification can endanger potential victims, and that concern is not discounted. But continuing registration and law-enforcement monitoring remain protective measures, while the State already marshals its initial factual case. A prompt adversarial determination under the heightened standard reduces erroneous classification without demanding perfect prediction or disabling warnings justified by the evidence. The required high-risk and low-risk overrides and individual factual review give the additional assurance practical work. Existing hearing procedures do not answer the separate question of ultimate persuasion and its strength. Sahhar preserves different burdens for different legal operations; this holding derives from this notification setting, not from treating its initial-commitment and discharge provisions as interchangeable. The Court imposes no universal heightened burden for every civil prediction.

**Judgment without a controlling plan-quantum rationale:** The injunction's requirement of clear and convincing State proof for the notification plan is also affirmed, 5–4, by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Only Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join Part III-B's plan-specific error-allocation reasoning. Stone-Zsela supports retention of that injunction component without adopting a plan-specific ground. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would retain State persuasion but permit preponderance. The injunction binds this litigation; no five-Justice plan-quantum rationale or broader general rule is manufactured from the judgment. There is no logical-subset combination of a reasonless judgment agreement and the four-Justice explanation under Marks.

### IV. The advance-notice emergency question remains unripe

**Holding and operative rule:** The present class challenge does not decide whether a concrete emergency may justify notification without ordinary advance notice because no representative alleges such notification and no prosecutor is shown to have done or planned it. The ordinary-process injunction is retained subject to that express reservation; it neither approves every emergency bypass nor prohibits every judicially authorized exception.

**Authority:** Part IV of Souter's opinion, joined by all seven other Associates. Stone-Zsela agrees with the disposition of the separately reserved emergency component, adding no emergency rationale or new exception.

**Controlling explanation:** The described mechanism permits a prosecutor to seek a judicial order when release information arrives only after a Tier 3 offender's release or the registrant evades service despite every good-faith effort; after three days without completed service the prosecutor may apply. Permission to apply is not a command to bypass notice. Without a concrete use or planned use affecting the class, the Court cannot determine the constitutional adequacy of that exceptional procedure or any narrowing state construction. A later concrete application must stand on its own facts and legal basis. The ordinary holding therefore resolves neither that future controversy nor an imagined automatic emergency exemption.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Ursery, Ward and Mendoza-Martinez supply rebuttable civil classification and combined purpose/effect examination; neither labels nor a single indicator is conclusive.
- Hendricks retains its as-applied punitive-confinement holding and actual-operation method; its outcome is distinguished, not replaced with an approval of that custody.
- Hudson preserves aggregate examination and Halper in its separate personal-monetary field. Halper is not extended into a notification accounting test.
- Kurth Ranch retains its extraordinary-tax punishment holding; its arrest-linked operation differs from the tailored warnings here.
- Sandin's substantive-constraint principle informs the protected state interest without transplanting a prison threshold into all civil settings. Paul v. Davis's reputation-alone boundary remains intact.
- Mathews supplies the context-specific process comparison. Addington and Santosky support attention to serious and irreversible error without creating a universal civil proof quantum.
- Sahhar preserves the distinct statutory initial-commitment and discharge burdens; neither is mechanically imported.
- Blockburger and retained Grady offense-identity questions are not reached. No precedent is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

Civil classification remains rebuttable by clearest proof of punitive combined operation. A genuine substantive state privacy constraint supports ordinary advance review and State persuasion for both tier and plan. Clear and convincing proof for the factual basis and risk classification is a five-Justice rule. The plan requirement remains part of the affirmed injunction, with no five-Justice plan-specific rationale. The emergency question and separate E.B. jurisdictional judgment remain outside the merits resolution.

#### Separate Writings

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment.** Stone-Zsela joins the civil-classification and heightened risk-classification portions. Public protection and a civil structure do not remove the need for timely notice, disclosure of the basis, an opportunity to contest, a neutral decisionmaker, written reasons and clear and convincing State proof before the broad notification at issue. The State controls the evidence and proposes the classification; an erroneous high tier can irreversibly affect housing, work, safety and status. A prompt adversarial process can reduce error without defeating protection. His express affirmance includes retention of the notification-plan injunction, but he adopts no plan-specific explanation and does not join the separate state-entitlement analysis. On the unripe emergency component he agrees only with the disposition and adds no emergency ground. His stated safeguards supply no majority adoption of a new general written-reasons or disclosure code. Confidential registration and lower-tier treatment remain subject to their own law; every internet registry, lifetime classification without review and affirmatively punitive operation remain unresolved.

**Stevens, dissenting in part.** Stevens would reverse the denial of Ex Post Facto relief and require an injunction against retrospective Tier 2/3 notification for this defined class. The affirmative official broadcast of conviction and predicted dangerousness, its criminal-history trigger and enduring cumulative burdens resemble imposed shaming. Risk and audience limits deserve weight but do not alter that combined character on his assessment. Ursery's dissenting approach and the actual-operation holdings of Hendricks and Hudson support looking beyond the civil label. He does not attribute every private attack to the State or decide independent Double Jeopardy offense identity. Because the Court leaves civil notification available, he joins the indicated process portions, including clear and convincing proof for both tier and plan.

**Souter's Part III-B, joined by Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer.** These four would apply clear and convincing persuasion to the plan as well as the classification because unnecessary geographic or audience expansion causes the same irreversible disclosure. The State prepares the plan and its initial justification; factual disputes, atypical risks and the actual likely-encounter limit make stronger assurance useful without demanding certainty. Continuing registration and monitoring reduce the comparative cost of mistaken undernotification. This is the rationale of four Justices, not a controlling general plan-quantum rule.

**Scalia, joined by Thomas; O'Connor and Kennedy join the proof-quantum portion only.** Scalia and Thomas reject the Ex Post Facto challenge because the particular risk-tailored warning scheme is genuinely civil and protective on this record. They separately reject the Double Jeopardy challenge because that civil warning process is not a successive criminal prosecution. They preserve their Hudson disagreement with a freestanding Halper civil multiple-punishment method; that view does not overrule Halper. All four proof-quantum dissenters accept the substantive state interest, advance opportunity and State persuasion for both tier and plan, but would permit preponderance. Mathews also accounts for potential victims, the danger of underclassification and existing safeguards. Noncustodial tailored warnings do not impose Addington's physical custody or Santosky's family-status severance; neither serious consequences nor a protected interest mechanically requires heightened certainty. Sahhar's different commitment and discharge rules demonstrate the need to preserve the actual legal operation. Their proposed modification would remove only the heightened quantum, preserving the remainder of the ordinary-process injunction.

#### Procedure After Action

The W.P. injunction remains in force: ordinary Tier 2/3 notification for this class requires advance opportunity to contest tier and plan and clear and convincing State persuasion for each. The expressly unripe emergency question remains reserved. Further relief is denied within the reviewed class; no individual risk assessment or notification plan is approved.

#### Source Notes

The [amended Third Circuit opinion, 119 F.3d 1077](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/119/119.F3d.1077.html), supplies the separate E.B. and W.P. appeals, class limits, scheme, individual-review rules, reported effects, process injunction and unripe emergency issue. The operative statute and Guidelines are described through that published account. The nineteen experiences, six compelled disclosures and 135 notifications are distinct populations; no combined incidence or causation finding is made.

### Hetzel v. Prince William County, No. 97-954. — 1998-03-23

#### Event

Hetzel v. Prince William County, No. 97-954. Summary merits decision, March 23, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 5. Following the separate same-date limited grant, the Court reviews the Fourth Circuit's mandamus command requiring an unconditional reduced compensatory judgment and staying a damages retrial. No oral argument is held. A $750,000 jury award was first reduced to $500,000 because one supporting claim was legally insufficient; after appellate excessiveness review, the District Court set $50,000 and permitted a new damages trial when Hetzel rejected it. The challenged mandamus foreclosed that option. A later $15,000 judgment and its separate pending appeal are not the judgment reviewed here.

#### Participation

All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

#### Public Action

The challenged mandamus judgment is reversed insofar as it forecloses the remittitur election, and the case is remanded for proceedings consistent with that ruling.

#### Judgment & Remedy

**Reversed in the reviewed respect and remanded, 9–0. Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. The mandamus constraint is removed insofar as it requires an unconditional reduced compensatory award and bars the jury election. Further proceedings must permit acceptance of a properly determined remittitur or an appropriate new trial, with damages-only retrial dependent on separability. No amount is selected, original verdict restored, claim revived or separate pending appeal decided.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Per curiam | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Reaches later mandamus challenge | Limited earlier-petition/mandate-scope ground; Stone-Zsela agrees with disposition only |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Per curiam | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Reverses the constraint and remands | Common remittitur election, remedy and stated limits |

No separate writing is filed. The merits joins disclose no certiorari poll.

#### Holdings

### I. The earlier-petition objection does not bar review of this later restriction

**Holding and operative rule:** Respondents' objection that the earlier petition omitted the jury-election claim does not prevent review of the later mandamus command here. The earlier mandate required recalculation without necessarily eliminating a remittitur election; the constitutional objection was before the Court of Appeals when its later order expressly required final judgment and stayed retrial.

**Authority:** Part I of the per curiam opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices directly adopt this confined threshold ground. Stone-Zsela agrees with reaching the later challenge but adds no preservation ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Recalculation and compulsory acceptance are different instructions. A reduced award can remain conditional on the plaintiff's choice, so the earlier instruction did not necessarily impose the no-election restriction now challenged. After Hetzel rejected the revised sum, the District Court addressed the Seventh Amendment question and permitted a new damages trial. That memorandum and issue were before the Court of Appeals when mandamus required an unconditional final judgment and stayed the trial.

Sanford Fork & Tool distinguishes matters actually settled by a mandate from those left open and permits examination of the opinion to determine its reach. Messenger distinguishes law-of-the-case practice from a jurisdictional limit on the rendering court's power. Neither excuses every omitted issue in an earlier petition. They support identifying what the earlier mandate actually determined; this sequence identifies the later no-election command as the challenged restriction.

Respondents correctly observe that a later enforcement order does not always reopen an earlier conclusive decision. That principle does not establish such a prior decision here. The Court does not reopen the earlier excessiveness determination, infer an unquoted contrary mandate term or find a general waiver exception. The separate pending appeal from the later $15,000 judgment neither erases this concrete restriction nor becomes part of this review.

### II. An excessiveness remittitur must preserve the new-trial election

**Holding and operative rule:** A federal court may condition retention of a jury's compensatory judgment on acceptance of a lawful reduction for excessiveness, but it may not impose that substituted valuation unconditionally while denying the plaintiff the option of a new jury trial. The challenged mandamus restriction is reversed insofar as it requires unconditional reduced recovery and forecloses that election, and the case is remanded for proceedings consistent with the choice between a properly determined remittitur and an appropriate new trial.

**Authority:** Part II of the per curiam opinion, joined by all nine Justices: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. This common election floor controls without requiring adoption of each Justice's distinct position on the broader appellate-allocation question in Gasperini.

**Controlling explanation:** Gasperini expressly preserves the federal remittitur election. The choice allows lawful correction of excessiveness while preventing a court's valuation from becoming an unconditional replacement for the jury's. Dimick preserves the traditional remittitur distinction, and Kennon v. Gilmer recognizes the need to leave the new-trial choice when a court reduces a jury's award. Calling the restriction a mandate does not remove the jury protection.

The initial reduction from $750,000 to $500,000 because one supporting claim was legally insufficient differs from the later excessiveness-based reductions. Neely's liability-insufficiency setting does not justify replacing a supported-liability jury valuation without the election. No legally fixed recovery cap is established for the challenged restriction; comparisons with awards in other cases do not create one. BMW's state punitive-damages remedy likewise supplies no exception to this federal compensatory-jury rule.

The Court does not find the original award reasonable, restore $750,000 or $500,000, select $50,000 or $15,000, revive the legally insufficient claim or reverse the earlier excessiveness determination. The scope of any new trial must follow ordinary law, including separability from liability before a damages-only trial. The later $15,000 judgment and pending separate appeal are not themselves vacated or decided. This remand removes the unlawful mandamus constraint; it does not promise a particular amount or an impermissibly partial retrial.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Gasperini's remittitur election is applied; its distinct diversity/state-compensation holding and existing federal appellate-allocation rule remain unchanged.
- Dimick v. Schiedt preserves traditional remittitur and the separate prohibition on federal additur.
- Kennon v. Gilmer, 131 U.S. 22, supplies the election principle when judicial reduction substitutes for the jury's damages valuation.
- Neely v. Martin K. Eby Construction Co., 386 U.S. 317, is distinguished as a liability-insufficiency decision, not authority for compulsory excessiveness remittitur.
- BMW v. Gore retains its state punitive-damages remedy and does not displace this federal compensatory-jury protection.
- In re Sanford Fork & Tool Co., 160 U.S. 247, supplies the settled/open mandate distinction; Messenger v. Anderson, 225 U.S. 436, distinguishes law-of-the-case practice from jurisdiction. Neither creates a general excuse for omitted earlier-petition issues. No precedent is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

The existing federal remittitur election remains enforceable against an unconditional appellate mandate. Review of this later restriction does not create a general waiver exception or reopen every earlier mandate. The original excessiveness determination, legally insufficient claim and pending separate damages appeal retain their stated boundaries.

#### Separate Writings

No separate writing is filed.

#### Procedure After Action

The matter returns for lawful proceedings preserving the choice between a properly determined remittitur and an appropriate new jury trial. Any damages-only trial requires separability from liability. No award is selected or automatically restored, and the later $15,000 judgment and separate appeal are not themselves vacated or decided.

#### Source Notes

The [reported proceeding, 523 U.S. 208](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-208.pdf), supplies the mandamus sequence, respondents' earlier-petition objection and the distinct pending appeal. Original earlier-petition and mandamus filings are known through published recitations rather than reproduced originals. No separate damages appeal, additional claim or dollar amount is resolved by this review.

### United States v. Robinson; Fifth Circuit No. 96-11165. — 1998-03-23

#### Event

United States v. Robinson; Fifth Circuit No. 96-11165, judgment below 119 F.3d 1205. Plenary merits decision, March 23, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 5. On review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the August 8, 1997 judgment. The grant concerns facial and as-applied Commerce Clause objections to the Hobbs Act convictions, including the proposed requirement of a substantial individual effect and the derivative firearm objection. The convictions comprise conspiracy, aiding and abetting three business robberies, and aiding and abetting one firearm offense. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the convictions but separately vacated the sentence and remanded on the vulnerable-victim enhancement; that sentencing component is outside the grant. No separate Supreme Court docket or oral-argument date is established.

#### Participation

All nine Justices participate at submission and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

#### Public Action

The judgment sustaining the convictions is affirmed insofar as the grant concerns the Hobbs Act commerce challenge and the wholly derivative firearm objection.

#### Judgment & Remedy

| Component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Remedy or limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Facial and as-applied commerce challenge to the Hobbs Act robbery and conspiracy convictions | Affirmed in the reviewed respect, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Convictions remain effective against this commerce objection |
| Wholly derivative firearm commerce challenge | Affirmed in the reviewed respect, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Stone-Zsela agrees with disposition only; no independent firearm defect is adjudicated |

The Fifth Circuit's separate sentencing vacatur and resentencing mandate remain undisturbed. The Court does not reinstate the vacated sentence or enhancement, order a new trial or new sentencing proceeding, or adjudicate an unrelated indictment, instruction or sufficiency objection.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Rejects the Hobbs Act commerce objections | Direct commercial-interference mechanism, aggregation after connection, robbery/conspiracy application and limits |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Kennedy | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Rejects the derivative firearm objection | Dependent constitutional ground only; Stone-Zsela agrees with this judgment component without joining its reasoning |

No separate writing is filed.

#### Holdings

### I. Direct interference with operating commercial assets supplies the required commerce connection

**Holding and operative rule:** Congress may apply the Hobbs Act to robbery directed at the operating assets of an active business participating in interstate commerce when the taking directly impairs its commercial operations and the Act's enacted commerce element is actually established. The effect of one robbery may be slight: aggregation measures the magnitude of this directly connected economic class, but neither a business label nor generalized economic consequences of crime supplies the antecedent connection.

**Authority:** Part I of Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; all nine directly adopt the rule, application to the Hobbs Act components and limits.

**Controlling explanation:** Lopez requires the enacted class and its actual interstate mechanism before magnitude can establish federal authority. The relevant class here is robbery affecting commerce through direct interference with operating business capital, not all robbery. The targeted businesses purchased interstate inventory and cashed out-of-state, payroll and government-benefit checks. The takings removed money withdrawn for those operations and impaired restocking and check-cashing capacity; the published record also reports one business closing for lack of capital. Taking the working money in a bank drive-through lane or store parking lot does not change its established business function.

American Life League supplies the closest mechanism: conduct directed at an actual interstate market's operations can directly obstruct that market. Once that relationship exists, Wickard and Perez permit evaluation of class-wide effects without demanding a substantial effect from each individual act. The statutory commerce element still requires an actual offense-specific nexus. Its words alone would not validate a constitutionally inadequate connection, and its character as an element does not make it subject-matter jurisdiction.

The contrary argument properly rejects multiplying local losses as a substitute for a constitutional mechanism. But this record identifies that mechanism before aggregation. A theory treating every victim as a potential consumer or every dollar as eventual interstate spending would lack this boundary and is not adopted. Hale, Rybar and Kirk concern the distinct inclusion of possession necessary to a valid machinegun regime; no such anti-evasion rationale is needed here.

The facial commerce objection fails because the Act lawfully reaches this defined class; the Court does not validate every imagined application. The actual business-robbery components and conspiracy directed at those robberies likewise require no substantial individual effect. This is no universal conspiracy-elements rule. Purely personal or household robbery, remote historical movement, every asserted depletion theory, a universal dollar floor and constitutional validity without the enacted commerce connection remain undecided.

### II. The wholly derivative firearm objection fails with the predicate commerce challenge

**Holding and operative rule:** The presented constitutional objection to the firearm conviction supplies no ground for relief because it depends entirely on the rejected claim that the underlying Hobbs Act business robberies exceed the commerce power. This disposition adjudicates no independent firearm element, instruction, sufficiency, aiding-and-abetting or collateral defect.

**Authority:** Part II of Kennedy's opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices directly adopt this derivative ground. Stone-Zsela agrees with the firearm disposition only and adds no ground.

**Controlling explanation:** The lower opinion identifies the firearm constitutional challenge as dependent on invalidity of the Hobbs Act predicates. Part I rejects that asserted invalidity through the actual business-interference mechanism and proved commerce nexus. The derivative argument therefore fails on its own stated premise. Neither this conclusion nor Salinas's distinct statutory-conspiracy analysis resolves an independent defect that is not presented. The Court does not infer a new admission, revise the indictment or approve the whole jury charge. The separate lower sentencing vacatur remains effective; the commerce affirmance neither reinstates the vulnerable-victim enhancement nor creates a new resentencing or retrial order.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Lopez is applied without changing its connection-before-magnitude sequence, actual statutory-class inquiry, fit requirement or rejection of a general police power. An enacted commerce element is relevant but no automatic safe harbor.
- American Life League supplies the direct-market-interference mechanism; its service-market application is extended to the actual impairment of these businesses' commercial operations, not to all crime costs.
- Wickard and Perez preserve class-wide magnitude analysis once a genuine economic-market connection exists; neither requires substantial individual magnitude or manufactures a missing connection.
- Hale, Rybar and Kirk retain their distinct anti-evasion/material-impairment ground for the machinegun regime. That ground is not transferred to robbery.
- Parker and Mussari/Schroeder retain the distinct cross-border-payment mechanism, and Pic-A-State retains its actual interstate-transmission ground; none supplies an all-money rule.
- Salinas's agreement analysis remains statute-specific and supplies no universal conspiracy code. Robertson's direct-enterprise alternative is not reached. No precedent is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

Robbery directly impairing the actual commercial operations of an interstate business may be regulated when the enacted Hobbs Act commerce connection is established. Aggregation addresses class-wide magnitude after that connection exists; no substantial individual effect is constitutionally required for this class. Purely personal robbery, generic consumer-spending chains and other reserved applications remain distinct. The firearm result is confined to the derivative objection, and the lower sentencing vacatur remains effective.

#### Separate Writings

No separate writing is filed.

#### Procedure After Action

This Supreme Court commerce review is complete. The convictions stand against these objections. The separate lower-court resentencing mandate continues under its own terms, without reinstatement of the vacated sentence or a new Supreme Court sentencing order.

#### Source Notes

The [official Fifth Circuit opinion, 119 F.3d 1205](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/96/96-11165.CR0.wpd.pdf), supplies the businesses' interstate inventory and check-cashing functions, targeted working-capital takings, commerce objections and separate sentencing vacatur. The [reported text](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/119/119.F3d.1205.96-11165.html) includes the complete lower analysis and footnotes. No exact dollar threshold, independent firearm defect, additional indictment finding or general instruction approval is supplied.


### Almendarez-Torres v. United States, No. 96-6839 — 1998-03-24

[Record](../records/almendarez_torres_v_united_states_merits_1998-03-24.md#public-projection)

#### Event

Almendarez-Torres v. United States, No. 96-6839. Argued October 14, 1997; decided March 24, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, reviewing its affirmance of an 85-month sentence. The question is whether the prior aggravated-felony conviction in 8 U.S.C. §1326(b)(2) is an element of aggravated unlawful reentry or a sentencing factor that need not appear in the indictment.

The September 1995 indictment charged unlawful reentry under §1326 without alleging the prior aggravated-felony convictions. At his December 1995 plea, Almendarez-Torres admitted the prior convictions and deportation; he preserved his objection that the indictment authorized no more than §1326(a)'s two-year maximum. The District Court imposed the enhanced sentence in March 1996.

#### Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision.

#### Public Action

The Court reverses the Fifth Circuit's judgment and remands for resentencing under the charged offense.

#### Judgment & Remedy

**Reversed and remanded, 5–4.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Souter and Ginsburg.
**Opposing:** O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer.

The enhanced sentence is vacated. On the existing indictment and plea, the sentence may not exceed §1326(a)'s two-year maximum. The guilty plea is not withdrawn and no acquittal is entered. Whether another source of law permits a further proceeding on a properly charged aggravated offense is not decided.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg | Statutory element classification, charging consequence and resentencing remedy |
| Opinion announcing the judgment, Part II | Scalia | Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg | Constitutional-avoidance explanation; no definitive constitutional classification rule |
| Concurrence in Part I and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Definitive constitutional ground for the element classification; does not join Part II's reservation of that question |
| Dissent | O'Connor | Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer | Penalty construction and bounded constitutional permission for this recidivist enhancement; would affirm |

#### Holdings

##### Section 1326(b)(2) requires an aggravated-offense allegation before its higher maximum may apply

**Holding and operative rule:** The prior aggravated-felony conviction specified in §1326(b)(2) is an element of the aggravated unlawful-reentry offense. It must be alleged in the federal indictment and, unless validly admitted as an element of the charged offense, proved to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt; an admission to the fact of a prior conviction does not cure its omission from this indictment, so the existing conviction permits no sentence above §1326(a)'s two-year maximum.

**Authority:** Part I of Scalia's opinion is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg. These five expressly adopt the statutory rule, its ordinary element consequences and the remedy. Four explain the construction through constitutional avoidance; Stone-Zsela gives a definitive constitutional ground separately. No majority adopts a general constitutional rule governing all facts that increase a statutory maximum.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that subsection (a)'s complete unlawful-reentry offense and two-year maximum must be distinguished from subsection (b)(2)'s aggravated offense carrying a twenty-year maximum. The prior conviction authorizes a different punishment ceiling; it does more than inform selection of punishment within the ordinary range. The provisions' cross-references permit that element construction. Hamling requires the indictment to state the offense's elements, and Gaudin requires proof of an actual element to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt when it has not validly been admitted. Almendarez-Torres admitted the prior convictions, but the indictment did not charge that aggravating element. His factual admission therefore does not answer the preserved objection to the punishment legally authorized by this charge.

The traditional use of recidivism at sentencing does not decide this statute's classification. McMillan addressed a minimum within an unchanged maximum, and Watts permits ordinary sentencing findings within conviction-based authority while reserving element evasion and other constitutional limits. Custis addresses collateral attacks on existing convictions, not the indictment's content. Old Chief confirms that prior-conviction status can be proved without unnecessary prejudicial detail; that evidentiary concern does not require treating status as a sentencing factor. The decision does not determine a subsidiary standard-of-proof claim, invalidate the admitted prior convictions, select a replacement sentence, or decide facts that do not increase the statutory maximum.

**Precedent treatment:** Hamling and Gaudin govern the consequences of the statutory classification; McMillan, Watts, Custis and Old Chief retain the distinct boundaries stated below.

#### Precedent Treatment

- **Hamling v. United States:** Applied to require an indictment alleging each element of the aggravated offense.
- **United States v. Gaudin:** Applied after statutory classification; its jury-and-proof rule for actual elements remains controlling without deciding all sentencing classifications.
- **McMillan v. Pennsylvania:** Distinguished because its mandatory minimum left the statutory maximum unchanged; its limited holding remains intact.
- **United States v. Watts / United States v. Putra:** Preserved for ordinary sentencing within punishment authorized by the conviction; it does not resolve this higher-maximum classification.
- **Custis v. United States:** Distinguished as a collateral-review decision; the existing limits on attacking prior convictions remain intact.
- **Old Chief v. United States:** Applied to the distinction between element status and the form of adequate prior-conviction proof; no broader compulsory-stipulation rule is created.

#### Law After Decision

Section 1326(b)(2)'s higher range requires the aggravated-offense element and the corresponding charging and proof protections. This statutory rule binds lower courts. The Court establishes no general constitutional prior-conviction exception and no general constitutional rule that every maximum-increasing fact is an element. Ordinary consideration of prior convictions within an independently authorized range remains available, subject to governing law.

#### Separate Writings

**Scalia, joined by Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg, Part II.** These Justices regard the tenfold increase in maximum punishment as presenting serious doubt about Congress's ability to assign the aggravating fact solely to a sentencing judge. The element reading is fairly available, so they apply constitutional avoidance and decline to decide that ultimate question. McMillan's unchanged ceiling and Watts's ordinary sentencing setting do not eliminate the doubt. The risk of prejudice from prior-conviction evidence can be addressed through adequate admissions or other proper proof rather than removal of an element from the charge.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in Part I and in the judgment.** The constitutional allocation turns on the fact's legal effect. A fact necessary to increase the authorized maximum from two years to twenty years performs the work of an element and must be charged and either validly admitted as an element of that offense or proved to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt. Legislative placement cannot transfer that work entirely to the sentencing judge. Gaudin protects element determination; Watts permits ordinary judicial sentencing findings only within conviction-based authority. Custis concerns collateral attack, and Old Chief demonstrates how adequate status proof can avoid unnecessary prejudice. The admitted facts here do not cure an indictment that never charged the aggravated offense. This position permits consideration of prior convictions within a separately authorized range, preserves Custis's collateral-review limits, requires no prejudicial details when adequate admission or stipulation establishes the element, and decides no sentencing fact that leaves the statutory maximum unchanged.

**O'Connor, joined by Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer, dissenting.** Subsection (b)(2)'s recidivist subject, reciprocal cross-references and punishment structure make it a penalty provision for the alien already described in subsection (a). Existing conviction status differs from facts about commission of the present crime, and Congress may treat that prior adjudication as a sentencing factor in this setting. The admission supports the application but is not a substitute for their statutory classification. These Justices acknowledge that McMillan and Watts do not alone resolve an increased ceiling; the distinct recidivism ground does that work. They would affirm without adopting unlimited legislative power to remove offense elements or resolving an unpresented subsidiary proof-burden question.

#### Procedure After Action

The case returns through the Fifth Circuit for resentencing. The enhanced sentence cannot remain in effect under the existing indictment and plea; the sentencing court must act within §1326(a)'s maximum. No new aggravated-offense proceeding or particular replacement term is ordered.

#### Source Notes

The applicable provision is the [1994 text of 8 U.S.C. §1326](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title8/pdf/USCODE-1994-title8.pdf), which increased the earlier fifteen-year aggravated-felony maximum to twenty years. The published account of the indictment, plea, preserved objection and sentence appears in [523 U.S. 227–229](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-224.pdf). That account does not establish the exact charged found-in date or an intentional waiver of the indictment objection. No temporal challenge or broader waiver is decided.

### Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, No. 96-1769 — 1998-03-25

[Record](../records/ohio_adult_parole_authority_v_woodard_merits_1998-03-25.md#public-projection)

#### Event

Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, No. 96-1769. Argued December 10, 1997; decided March 25, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Sixth Circuit, reviewing 107 F.3d 1178. The questions concern due process in Ohio's capital-clemency procedure and whether the offered interview compels self-incrimination.

Woodard brought this §1983 action after receiving notice of a voluntary interview and a clemency hearing. He did not request the interview. The District Court granted judgment on the pleadings. The Sixth Circuit rejected an independent entitlement to clemency, but ordered further proceedings on an established-process theory of due process and on a possible unconstitutional condition on silence.

#### Participation

All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

#### Public Action

The Court reverses the Sixth Circuit's directions for further proceedings on the presented due-process and self-incrimination claims.

#### Judgment & Remedy

| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Due-process remand | Reversed, 8–1 | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Stevens | Reject the present process claim; no entitlement to clemency or new hearing follows |
| Self-incrimination remand | Reversed, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | — | Reject the claim based on the offered voluntary interview |

The Sixth Circuit's rejection of an independent entitlement to clemency is undisturbed. The case returns for proceedings consistent with these rulings. The Court neither grants nor denies mercy, sets an execution date, adjudicates a stay, nor orders immunity or a new clemency hearing.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I-A | O'Connor | Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | No state-created substantive entitlement to clemency; Stone-Zsela joins the conclusion that discretionary mercy creates no right to its grant |
| Opinion of the Court, Part I-B | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Appellate analogy supplies no basis for the requested procedure; Stone-Zsela joins only the distinction between discretionary mercy and another criminal trial |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II-A | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Minimum safeguards against fundamentally arbitrary capital-clemency procedure |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II-B | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | The pleaded process objections do not establish violation of that minimum; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas agree in this disposition on Parts I-A and I-B |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III-A | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | The offered voluntary interview does not establish compelled self-incrimination |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III-B | O'Connor | Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | The conclusion also survives an assumed ordinary civil adverse inference, with actual-compulsion and automatic-penalty limits; Stone-Zsela does not join this additional ground |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Kennedy | Scalia and Thomas | Joins Parts I and III; rejects the present process claim without joining Part II's affirmative retained-life framework |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Stevens | No other Justice | Joins I-A, II-A and III; would preserve the due-process remand and does not join I-B or II-B |

#### Holdings

##### I. Required clemency procedures do not create an entitlement to mercy or triallike review

**Holding and operative rule:** Ohio's required investigation, hearing and advisory recommendation do not create a substantive entitlement to clemency because they do not constrain the Governor to grant it on specified facts. The analogy to a first appeal as of right does not itself require appellate representation, triallike evidence procedure or a new determination of guilt in this discretionary executive process.

**Authority:** Part I-A has all eight Associates, with Stone-Zsela also joining the no-right-to-mercy conclusion. Part I-B has O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; Stone-Zsela joins only the mercy-versus-criminal-trial distinction. Stevens does not join the rejection of the established-process analogy.

**Controlling explanation:** Dumschat distinguishes seeking clemency from entitlement to its grant. Sandin requires a genuine substantive constraint on a meaningful deprivation; Doe and Johnson likewise distinguish required administration from an entitlement to a favorable discretionary decision. Ohio must investigate, hold the required hearing and recommend action even after an execution stay, but its recommendation is advisory and the Governor retains complete discretion. A later hearing or revised recommendation on new information is permitted, not required. These provisions do not compel clemency.

Evitts protects the first appeal as of right within adjudication of guilt. Clemency performs a different executive function. Its availability after conviction does not itself import appellate or trial procedure. The Court rejects the Sixth Circuit's general integral-stage theory as a basis for the requested remand, while preserving independently retained constitutional rights. Herrera's record-specific innocence ruling establishes no rule that executive mercy is the exclusive constitutionally sufficient substitute for every claim of innocence.

##### II. Capital-clemency procedures retain a constitutional minimum, satisfied on these pleadings

**Holding and operative rule:** An established capital-clemency process must afford minimal safeguards against fundamentally arbitrary procedure, including arbitrary denial of any access or substitution of an entirely arbitrary device such as a coin flip for consideration. The notice and offered interview here, considered with the pleaded restrictions, satisfy that minimum; they establish no entitlement to clemency, trial protections, a favorable recommendation or judicial review of mercy's merits.

**Authority:** Part II-A's minimum safeguard has six direct joins: O'Connor, Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Part II-B's sufficient-process application has five: O'Connor, Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stevens disputes the application; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas agree with rejection of the claim on their distinct entitlement/adjudication ground. Both controlling propositions rest on direct majority joins, without combining separate rationales under Marks.

**Controlling explanation:** A valid death sentence reduces the process owed before discretionary mercy is denied, but the prisoner remains alive. That retained interest supplies a minimum protection independent of a state-created entitlement to release. Ford illustrates the distinction between the interest protected and the flexible procedure appropriate to it; this case does not import Ford's separate prohibition on executing an incompetent prisoner or its particular hearing requirements.

Woodard alleges three days' interview notice, ten days' hearing notice, difficulty preparing while postconviction proceedings continued, exclusion of counsel from the interview, chair-controlled counsel participation at the hearing, and inability to testify or submit documents at the hearing. Accepting that pleaded account, the notice and offered personal interview provided access, and those restrictions do not establish fundamentally arbitrary procedure requiring further adjudication. The Court does not find an unmentioned alternative document channel or reject the allegations as untrue. It establishes neither a fixed list of required safeguards nor an accuracy code for every disputed item in a clemency file. Johnson's rejection of a parole-file process entitlement does not extinguish independent constitutional protection.

##### III. The optional interview does not establish compelled self-incrimination

**Holding and operative rule:** An optional clemency interview does not compel self-incrimination merely because the prisoner must choose between providing potentially harmful information and remaining silent; absence of counsel, confidentiality or immunity does not itself convert this invitation into compulsion. The conclusion also holds if an ordinary civil adverse inference from silence is assumed, but it does not authorize an automatic privilege penalty, compelled waiver or criminal use of compelled answers.

**Authority:** Part III-A's present voluntary-interview holding has all nine Justices. Part III-B's additional ordinary-inference ground and its limits have all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela does not join that additional ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Murphy distinguishes a difficult evidentiary choice from a command backed by a genuine threatened penalty for asserting the privilege. Woodard was invited, not required, to attend or answer. The State's refusal to promise confidentiality or immunity does not establish that it compelled answers. No automatic loss of clemency eligibility for silence, compelled waiver or criminal use of compelled testimony is established.

The eight Associates additionally apply Baxter's distinction between ordinary adverse inferences in civil proceedings and automatic sanctions attached to silence. Even assuming such an inference in this civil clemency evaluation, the voluntary choice does not become compelled testimony. The record does not establish Ohio's actual use of silence or answers; the assumption supplies an alternative legal ground, not a factual finding. LaChance preserves separately supported compulsion and waiver claims, and Johnson confirms that absence of entitlement to a benefit does not excuse an independent unconstitutional penalty. A materially supported coercive condition would therefore require its own analysis.

#### Precedent Treatment

- **Connecticut Board of Pardons v. Dumschat:** Applied to discretionary mercy and the distinction between seeking relief and entitlement to its grant; not extended to extinguish independent constitutional interests.
- **Sandin v. Conner:** Applied at its substantive-constraint rule. Mandatory procedure alone is insufficient, and directly retained constitutional interests remain separate.
- **Doe v. District of Columbia:** Applied to distinguish investigative duties from a substantive entitlement.
- **Johnson v. Rodriguez:** Applied to the same procedure/entitlement boundary and preservation of independent constitutional wrongs; its ordinary initial-parole rule does not displace the retained-life floor.
- **Evitts v. Lucey:** Distinguished at the adjudicatory first appeal as of right; it does not itself require the requested capital-clemency procedures.
- **Ford v. Wainwright:** Its distinction between a protected interest and appropriate flexible procedure informs the minimum-process rule; its separate incompetency protection remains unchanged.
- **Herrera v. Collins:** Preserved as a record-specific innocence disposition; no exclusive-clemency rule is attributed to it.
- **Minnesota v. Murphy:** Applied to distinguish voluntary choices from supported threats of a privilege penalty.
- **Baxter v. Palmigiano:** Applied by the eight Associates to ordinary civil adverse inferences, distinct from automatic punishment or compelled criminal testimony.
- **LaChance v. Erickson / McManus:** Preserved for separately established compulsion and waiver; it supplies no general prohibition on lawful civil inferences.

#### Law After Decision

Capital clemency remains discretionary executive mercy, separate from judicial collateral review. Required administrative steps create no right to a favorable outcome. A directly controlling minimum protects remaining life against fundamentally arbitrary clemency procedure, but the pleaded restrictions here do not breach it. The optional interview establishes no compelled self-incrimination, including on the eight-Justice alternative assumption of an ordinary civil adverse inference. No general absence of constitutional protection is declared.

#### Separate Writings

**Kennedy, joined by Scalia and Thomas, concurring in part and in the judgment.** Ohio's procedure does not constrain the ultimate mercy decision, and the appellate analogy supplies no right to the process requested. Dumschat and the substantive distinction applied in Sandin and Johnson resolve these pleaded process claims. These Justices do not join the affirmative retained-life framework or its application; their judgment agreement adds no join to Part II. They preserve independently grounded constitutional prohibitions and fully join the self-incrimination analysis, including its actual-compulsion and automatic-penalty limits.

**Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** A prisoner remains alive, and an established procedure integral to the State's final decision to take life must afford basic fairness and meaningful participation. His Dumschat position and Evitts's established-process principle support bounded inquiry into the process as a whole, even though clemency need not replicate a trial and no right to mercy exists. He joins the minimum safeguard but would preserve the due-process remand to consider the relevant materials rather than hold these pleadings insufficient. He finds no violation already established and prescribes none of the requested safeguards automatically. He joins both self-incrimination grounds, distinguishing this voluntary invitation from a command backed by a serious threatened sanction.

#### Procedure After Action

The Sixth Circuit must conform its disposition to rejection of the presented due-process and self-incrimination claims. Its no-entitlement ruling stands. The decision neither retries guilt nor prevents lawful executive clemency review under Ohio's existing duties; it orders no particular recommendation, hearing, release, stay or execution.

#### Source Notes

The state procedure, judgment-on-the-pleadings posture, Sixth Circuit rulings and asserted deficiencies appear in [523 U.S. 276–279 and 289–290](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-272.pdf). The same source at 286 identifies the absence of a record showing actual use of answers or silence and the Authority's refusal to promise confidentiality or immunity. The pleaded limitations are evaluated as allegations, not resolved against Woodard through new factual findings. No equal-protection claim is presented.

### Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc., No. 96-1768 — 1998-03-31

[Record](../records/feltner_v_columbia_pictures_television_inc_merits_1998-03-31.md#public-projection)

#### Event

Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc., No. 96-1768. Argued January 21, 1998; decided March 31, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, reviewing 106 F.3d 284. The question is whether §504(c) of the Copyright Act or the Seventh Amendment entitles Feltner to a jury determination of statutory damages.

After license termination, the stations continued broadcasting Columbia's programs. The District Court granted summary judgment on infringement liability, denied Feltner's jury demand and, after a bench trial, found willfulness and 440 infringements. It selected $20,000 for each, totaling $8.8 million. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the relevant damages rulings but separately vacated the costs-and-fees award for explanation. Only Columbia's copyright claims against Feltner remained.

#### Participation

All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

#### Public Action

The Court reverses the denial of a jury determination of statutory damages and remands.

#### Judgment & Remedy

**Reversed and remanded, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The judge-selected statutory-damages determinations are vacated. On the timely demand, factual issues pertinent to statutory damages, including willfulness and the amount within the lawful range, must be submitted to a jury. The court retains its legal, sufficiency and lawful review functions. Unreviewed infringement liability is not reopened; the separate costs-and-fees remand remains. No lawful work count, willfulness finding, replacement amount or lower ultimate award is predetermined.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | No statutory jury entitlement; constitutional allocation of statutory-damages facts and amount; bounded reversal and remand |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Scalia | No other Justice | Reads §504(c) itself to preserve the jury function and avoids deciding the constitutional question |

#### Holdings

##### Section 504(c) supplies no independent statutory jury entitlement

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 504(c)'s authorization of statutory damages does not itself confer a right to a jury determination. That statutory conclusion does not settle the separate Seventh Amendment allocation.

**Authority:** Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: eight direct joins.

**Controlling explanation:** The provision supplies a damages election, ranges and specific conditions for adjustment. Its references to what the court considers just, the court's findings and its discretion contain no independent jury command. Reading those references in the context of the whole subsection yields no statutory entitlement to jury assessment. The contrary institutional reading of court cannot displace that conclusion merely to avoid the constitutional issue. The Court must therefore determine whether the Constitution preserves the jury's role despite the statute's allocation; statutory silence about a jury does not eliminate constitutional protection.

##### The Seventh Amendment protects the initial determination of statutory-damages facts and amount

**Holding and operative rule:** On a timely jury demand in this private copyright statutory-damages action, the Seventh Amendment assigns disputed factual issues pertinent to the award, including willfulness and the amount within the lawful statutory range, to the jury. The court continues to interpret the statute, identify the lawful range, decide legal sufficiency and conduct constitutionally permissible review; the ruling does not assign injunctions, fees, costs, equitable accountings or historically judicial questions to juries.

**Authority:** The same eight Justices join the Court's constitutional holding and damages remand. Scalia supports the judgment on the separate statutory ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Copyright damages have a historical legal analogue, and the monetary remedy seeks compensation or punishment of the kind traditionally assessed by a jury. A range requiring judgment does not turn that task into equitable relief. Markman's historical and functional inquiry distinguishes a legal action's jury protection from the assignment of a particular legal-meaning function; its judicial patent-construction rule does not transfer disputed damages valuation to a judge.

Tull's allocation of the amount of a governmental civil penalty does not control this private copyright-damages function. Congress may identify the lawful range without removing the jury's task of deciding the pertinent facts and selecting the amount within it. Gasperini and Hetzel concern lawful review and the new-trial election after an award; they do not authorize initial judicial substitution for the demanded jury. Their applicable review limits remain intact.

Feltner demanded a jury, but the judge decided willfulness and the statutory amount. Those determinations cannot stand on that procedure. The remand changes the decisionmaker for the protected work, not the statute's ranges, burdens, per-work unit or exceptions. It does not resolve every challenge to the count of works, reopen unreviewed liability or guarantee any particular award.

**Operative statutory qualifications:** The owner may elect statutory damages before final judgment instead of actual damages and profits. The ordinary range is $500–$20,000 for all infringements of any one work for which one infringer is individually liable or two or more infringers are jointly and severally liable; all parts of a compilation or derivative work are one work. Owner-proved willfulness permits, but does not require, an increase to $100,000. Infringer-proved lack of awareness and of reason to believe the acts infringed permits, but does not require, reduction to no less than $200.

Mandatory remission is a separate rule. It requires belief, with reasonable grounds, that the use was fair use under §107, and either (1) reproduction in copies or phonorecords by an employee or agent of a nonprofit educational institution, library or archives acting within employment, or by that institution, library or archives itself; or (2) performance of a published nondramatic literary work, or reproduction of a transmission program embodying its performance, by a public broadcasting entity as defined in §118(g), or by a person as a regular part of that entity's nonprofit activities. Innocence or broadcaster status alone does not satisfy this rule. The Court finds no exception established here.

#### Precedent Treatment

- **Markman v. Westview Instruments:** Applied at its history-and-function method and distinction between legal construction and protected factual work; its patent-construction allocation remains intact.
- **Tull v. United States:** Distinguished at the governmental civil-penalty amount function; it is not overruled or extended to private copyright damages.
- **Gasperini v. Center for Humanities:** Preserved for lawful trial-court review and bounded appellate review; its diversity-law rule supplies no copyright valuation formula.
- **Hetzel v. Prince William County:** Preserved for the choice between lawful excessiveness remittitur and an appropriate new jury trial, with separability required for damages-only retrial; it does not authorize the initial bench assessment here.

#### Law After Decision

A timely jury demand protects the statutory-damages facts and amount in a private copyright damages action. The statute's substantive limits remain in force, and ordinary legal and constitutionally permissible review functions remain judicial. The prior description of this monetary relief as equitable cannot sustain the denial of the demanded jury. No constitutional ruling about every civil penalty, fee, cost or equitable remedy follows.

#### Separate Writings

**Scalia, concurring in the judgment.** The word court can refer to the lawful tribunal, including its jury. Reading §504(c) to preserve jury determination of damages facts and amount fits that institutional use and avoids an unnecessary constitutional decision. His Tull position distinguishes Congress's power to fix an amount from authority to remove an unfixed legal award from the jury. He therefore agrees with reversal and the jury-damages remand, but does not join the Court's contrary statutory premise or reach its constitutional holding. This difference does not alter the statutory ranges, exceptions or the remand's limits.

#### Procedure After Action

The case returns for a jury determination of the protected statutory-damages issues on the timely demand, subject to lawful rulings on statutory meaning, sufficiency and review. The existing damages award is not reinstated, a replacement amount is not selected, and the separate costs-and-fees remand remains for its own consideration.

#### Source Notes

The applicable damages amounts and separate qualifications appear in the [1994 text of 17 U.S.C. §504](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title17/pdf/USCODE-1994-title17-chap5-sec504.pdf). The party, liability and bench-damages history and separate fees disposition are reported at [523 U.S. 342–345](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-340.pdf). The 440-infringement and willfulness determinations are those of the lower court; they are not findings newly made here.

### Texas v. United States, No. 97-29 — 1998-03-31

[Record](../records/texas_v_united_states_threshold_1998-03-31.md#public-projection)

#### Event

Texas v. United States, No. 97-29. Argued January 14, 1998; decided March 31, 1998. On appeal from the three-judge United States District Court for the District of Columbia. Texas seeks a declaration that §5 of the Voting Rights Act does not apply to school-district interventions authorized by Texas Education Code §§39.131(a)(7) and (8). It argues both that these interventions do not change voting and that they accord with federal education-grant conditions. The District Court dismissed the action as unripe without deciding either merits theory.

#### Participation

All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

#### Public Action

The Court affirms the dismissal for lack of a ripe controversy.

#### Judgment & Remedy

**Affirmed, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The requested declaration remains unavailable in this unripe action. Neither the voting-coverage theory nor the federal-funding theory is adjudicated. No injunction, exemption or merits remand is ordered; review remains available when a sufficiently definite intervention produces a concrete controversy.

#### Opinion Topology

Stevens delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. No separate writing is filed.

#### Holdings

##### A categorical preclearance exemption is unripe before the challenged intervention is sufficiently defined

**Holding and operative rule:** A request to exempt possible future school-district interventions from §5 is unripe when no sufficiently definite intervention, affected district or allocation of powers establishes a fit legal controversy and no substantial present hardship justifies deciding before those details exist. Texas's challenge therefore must be dismissed without deciding whether any particular intervention changes voting or whether a supported federal-funding conflict affects that question.

**Authority:** Stevens's Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices: nine direct joins.

**Controlling explanation:** Abbott Laboratories requires attention to fitness for decision and the hardship of withholding review. The Commissioner has not selected a currently foreseen or likely district for the challenged master or management-team appointments. Under the recited state policy, lesser sanctions would first be tried; even then the Commissioner selects intervention only to the extent necessary and defines the appointees' actual powers. The legal significance of that implementation cannot be resolved through a universal exemption.

Presley requires a direct relation to voting and leaves extreme displacement of elective authority unresolved. Texas law independently prohibits these appointees from acting concerning a district election, changing the board's size or selection method, setting a tax rate, or adopting a budget with a spending level different from the level set by the board. Those limits do not themselves establish every future appointment's effect. The Attorney General's warning that some implementations could require preclearance is not a determination that an identified voting change occurred.

New York permitted review because the future obligation required substantial present preparations; Pic-A-State involved an existing business stopped by a real criminal constraint. Texas shows no comparable present burden. Its earlier Dallas County request and ninety-day approval period do not establish a current appointment, inevitable delay or present voting change. The Court does not require a party to violate the law before challenging a concrete obligation. It requires the controversy here to become sufficiently definite. Neither federal-grant compatibility nor voting coverage is reached, and Raines's rule for individual legislators is not a prohibition on suits by States.

#### Precedent Treatment

- **Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner:** Applied at the fitness-and-hardship inquiry; uncertainty alone does not require an advisory declaration.
- **New York v. United States:** Distinguished because its future command already required substantial present siting action; timely pre-enforcement review remains available in that setting.
- **Pic-A-State Pennsylvania v. Reno:** Distinguished because an actual criminal constraint had already stopped the plaintiff's existing business; no prosecution prerequisite is added.
- **Presley v. Etowah County Commission / Mack v. Russell County Commission:** Preserved at its direct voting-relation rule and reservation concerning effective replacement of elected authority; no future intervention is classified here.
- **Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment:** Applied to require the Article III inquiry before contested statutory merits.
- **Raines v. Byrd:** Its concrete-injury discipline is respected without extending its individual-legislator rule into a categorical bar on governmental plaintiffs.

#### Law After Decision

The dismissal creates no substantive exemption for school-district interventions and no blanket prohibition on pre-enforcement review. Existing §5 law continues to govern an actual covered change. A sufficiently definite later intervention and real dispute may support review through the proper statutory channel; its coverage and any supported federal-funding question remain open.

#### Separate Writings

No separate writing is filed.

#### Procedure After Action

The District Court's ripeness dismissal stands. Texas receives no advisory coverage ruling or authorization to implement an unidentified change. Any later controversy must satisfy the ordinary jurisdictional and statutory requirements on its own actual facts.

#### Source Notes

The statutory powers and restrictions, administrative correspondence, two grounds for the requested declaration, implementation contingencies and prior Dallas County example appear in [523 U.S. 297–301](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-296.pdf). Trying lesser sanctions first is a recited state policy and complaint premise, not a new command attributed to §§39.131(a)(7) or (8). The separate election, board-composition, tax-rate and budget prohibitions arise from §39.131(e).

### United States v. Scheffer, No. 96-1133 — 1998-03-31

[Record](../records/united_states_v_scheffer_merits_1998-03-31.md#public-projection)

#### Event

United States v. Scheffer, No. 96-1133. Argued November 3, 1997; decided March 31, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces under 28 U.S.C. §1259, reviewing 44 M.J. 442. The question is whether Military Rule of Evidence 707's categorical exclusion of polygraph evidence violates the accused's constitutional right to present a defense.
